claim: Working memory is the ability to temporarily maintain and mentally manipulate information and is fundamental to cognition.
source: Working memory, the ability to temporarily maintain and mentally manipulate information, is fundamental to cognition (Baddeley, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baddeley, 1986

claim: Working memory requires communication across distributed brain regions.
source: This ability is known to require communication across distributed brain regions and is conserved over mammalia (Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Lee and Kesner, 2003; Winter and Stich, 2005; Wang and Cai, 2006; Eichenbaum, 2008; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Christophel et al., 2017; Eichenbaum, 2017; Churchwell and Kesner, 2011; Spellman et al., 2015; Hallock et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2015; Bolkan et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2018; Maisson et al., 2018; Lugtmeijer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Working memory is conserved over mammalia.
source: This ability is known to require communication across distributed brain regions and is conserved over mammalia (Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Lee and Kesner, 2003; Winter and Stich, 2005; Wang and Cai, 2006; Eichenbaum, 2008; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Christophel et al., 2017; Eichenbaum, 2017; Churchwell and Kesner, 2011; Spellman et al., 2015; Hallock et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2015; Bolkan et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2018; Maisson et al., 2018; Lugtmeijer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Long-range interactions are thought to be supported by the proper timing of action potentials (spikes).
source: Long-range interactions are thought to be supported by the proper timing of action potentials (spikes), and brain rhythms are thought to act as a clocking mechanism to synchronize the timing of spike discharges (Fries, 2005; Buzsáki, 2006; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Colgin, 2011; Fries, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Brain rhythms are thought to act as a clocking mechanism to synchronize the timing of spike discharges.
source: Long-range interactions are thought to be supported by the proper timing of action potentials (spikes), and brain rhythms are thought to act as a clocking mechanism to synchronize the timing of spike discharges (Fries, 2005; Buzsáki, 2006; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Colgin, 2011; Fries, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in rats.
source: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in rats (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993), primates (Jutras et al., 2009), and humans (Qasim et al., 2021), although the exact frequency can vary over mammalia.
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993

claim: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in primates.
source: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in rats (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993), primates (Jutras et al., 2009), and humans (Qasim et al., 2021), although the exact frequency can vary over mammalia.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jutras et al., 2009

claim: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in humans.
source: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in rats (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993), primates (Jutras et al., 2009), and humans (Qasim et al., 2021), although the exact frequency can vary over mammalia.
evidence: Supported by citation to Qasim et al., 2021

claim: The exact frequency of LFP-spike coupling can vary over mammalia.
source: Fluctuations in the local field potential (LFP) are coupled to the organization of hippocampal spiking activity in rats (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993), primates (Jutras et al., 2009), and humans (Qasim et al., 2021), although the exact frequency can vary over mammalia.
evidence: Stated as a qualification to the LFP-spike coupling observation

claim: The hypothesis that brain rhythms coordinate brain communication by synchronizing neuronal activity is known as 'communication through coherence'.
source: The hypothesis that brain rhythms coordinate brain communication by synchronizing neuronal activity, known as 'communication through coherence', is just beginning to be experimentally tested (Fries, 2005; Buzsáki, 2006; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Fries, 2015; Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The 'communication through coherence' hypothesis is just beginning to be experimentally tested.
source: The hypothesis that brain rhythms coordinate brain communication by synchronizing neuronal activity, known as 'communication through coherence', is just beginning to be experimentally tested (Fries, 2005; Buzsáki, 2006; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Fries, 2015; Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: In rats, computations within and communication between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and hippocampus are required for spatial working memory.
source: In rats, decades of research have shown that computations within, and communication between, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and hippocampus are required for spatial working memory (Dudchenko et al., 2000; Lee and Kesner, 2003; Wang and Cai, 2006; Horst and Laubach, 2009; Churchwell and Kesner, 2011; Hallock et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Recording studies implicate theta synchrony within the mPFC-hippocampal network as a mechanism for mPFC-hippocampal communication.
source: Recording studies specifically implicate theta synchrony within the mPFC-hippocampal network as a mechanism for mPFC-hippocampal communication.
evidence: Stated as a summary of recording studies

claim: mPFC-hippocampal coherence has been repeatedly correlated with memory-guided choices.
source: One metric of oscillatory synchrony, coherence, has been repeatedly correlated with memory-guided choices (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Benchenane et al., 2010; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016), but also with attention and task engagement (Guise and Shapiro, 2017; Bygrave et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: mPFC-hippocampal coherence has been correlated with attention and task engagement.
source: One metric of oscillatory synchrony, coherence, has been repeatedly correlated with memory-guided choices (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Benchenane et al., 2010; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016), but also with attention and task engagement (Guise and Shapiro, 2017; Bygrave et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guise and Shapiro, 2017; Bygrave et al., 2019

claim: 4–12 Hz mPFC-hippocampal coherence was stronger before rats made a correct choice when compared to a choice error or a forced navigation trial on a spatial memory task.
source: In a cornerstone experiment, Jones and Wilson, 2005, showed that 4–12 Hz mPFC-hippocampal coherence was stronger before rats made a correct choice when compared to a choice error or a forced navigation trial on a spatial memory task.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones and Wilson, 2005

claim: Magnitude squared coherence is a measurement of signal correlation with no requirement for exact numerical phase consistency.
source: Importantly, these results are derived from measurements of magnitude squared coherence, a measurement of signal correlation, with no requirement for exact numerical phase consistency.
evidence: Stated as a definition of magnitude squared coherence

claim: Two structures can exhibit strong magnitude squared coherence despite two signals being approximately 180 degree offset in phase.
source: For example, two structures can exhibit strong magnitude squared coherence, despite two signals being approximately 180 degree offset in phase.
evidence: Stated as an example to illustrate the properties of magnitude squared coherence

claim: There currently exist two versions of the communication through coherence hypothesis: first, that inter-areal communication varies with signal phase, irrespective of coherence, and second that inter-areal communication varies with coherence.
source: This is an important distinction because there currently exist two versions of the communication through coherence hypothesis; first, that inter-areal communication varies with signal phase, irrespective of coherence, and second that inter-areal communication varies with coherence (Vinck et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vinck et al., 2023

claim: The finding that mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence was stronger on correct choice outcomes is potentially conflated with the fact that rodent movement behaviors also change with task performance.
source: Likewise, the finding that mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence was stronger on correct choice outcomes is potentially conflated with the fact that rodent movement behaviors also change with task performance (Redish, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Redish, 2016

claim: It remains unclear as to whether strong theta coherence increased the likelihood of a correct choice, or whether a correct choice led to stronger theta coherence.
source: Due to constraints on experimental design, it remains unclear as to whether strong theta coherence increased the likelihood of a correct choice, or whether a correct choice led to stronger theta coherence.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge based on experimental design constraints

claim: Addressing whether strong theta coherence increases the likelihood of a correct choice is of critical importance for the potential use of oscillatory dynamics in therapeutic settings.
source: Addressing this question is of critical importance for the potential use of oscillatory dynamics in therapeutic settings (Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019

claim: If magnitude squared coherence represents a valid mechanism for prefrontal-hippocampal communication, then using times of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence to gate access to the choice would be associated with better performance on memory-guided tasks.
source: We hypothesized that if magnitude squared coherence represents a valid mechanism for prefrontal-hippocampal communication, that we could use times of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence to gate access to the choice, and that these trials would be associated with better performance on memory-guided tasks.
evidence: Stated as the authors' hypothesis

claim: Trials initiated during times of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence were associated with correct choice outcomes on both spatial working memory-dependent and -independent tasks.
source: Trials initiated during times of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence were associated with correct choice outcomes on both spatial working memory-dependent and -independent tasks.
evidence: Stated as a result from the brain-machine interface experiment

claim: mPFC theta rhythms and mPFC-thalamic interactions increased with mPFC-hippocampal theta synchrony.
source: In follow-up experiments, we found that mPFC theta rhythms and mPFC-thalamic interactions increased with mPFC-hippocampal theta synchrony.
evidence: Stated as a result from follow-up experiments

claim: Prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchronization leads to a higher probability of a correct choice.
source: Together, our results show that prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchronization leads to a higher probability of a correct choice and strengthens prefrontal-thalamic dialogue.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the results

claim: Prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchronization strengthens prefrontal-thalamic dialogue.
source: Together, our results show that prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchronization leads to a higher probability of a correct choice and strengthens prefrontal-thalamic dialogue.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the results

claim: Longer delay durations were associated with lower choice accuracy on the delayed alternation task.
source: Consistent with the use of delayed-response tasks across species (Dudchenko, 2004; Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Eichenbaum, 2008), longer delay durations were associated with lower choice accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and citations to published research

claim: There was a significant effect of delay duration on future choice outcomes during task training.
source: There was a significant effect of delay duration on future choice outcomes (F(5,35) = 3.38; repeated measures ANOVA; N=8 rats, 4 male, 4 female).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: There was a greater proportion of correct choices following short delays relative to long delays.
source: There was a greater proportion of correct choices following short delays relative to long delays (t(7) = 3.7, p=0.007, ci = [3.15, 14.1]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C

claim: Waiting 250 ms before extracting new signals provided reliable streaming between the brain and MATLAB.
source: By iteratively extracting signals into MATLAB from the Neuralynx acquisition system at systematically increasing lags (25–300 ms), we found that waiting 250 ms before extracting new signals provided reliable streaming between the brain and MATLAB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Dataset sizes strongly impacted the shape of the coherence distribution.
source: By linearly increasing the amount of data being analyzed, and calculating coherence over 50 separate intervals from an example rat in real time, we noticed that the dataset sizes strongly impacted the shape of the coherence distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), although the effect on coherence magnitude was less robust (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F

claim: The strongest frequency (4–12 Hz) plateaued at ~8 Hz when analyzing dataset sizes of 1.25 s.
source: Since the strongest frequency (4–12 Hz) plateaued at ~8 Hz when analyzing dataset sizes of 1.25 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), we chose to use 1.25 s dataset sizes with 250 ms steps forward in time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F

claim: Presenting trials during elevated states of mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence improved choice accuracy relative to yoked control trials.
source: Consistent with our first prediction, presenting trials during elevated states of mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence improved choice accuracy (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Choice accuracy on trials presented during states of low mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence did not differ from choice accuracy on yoked control trials.
source: However, choice accuracy on trials presented during states of low mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence did not differ from choice accuracy on yoked control trials, indicating that naturally occurring weak theta synchronization does not impair choice outcomes.
evidence: Stated as a result from the brain-machine interface experiment

claim: Naturally occurring weak theta synchronization does not impair choice outcomes.
source: However, choice accuracy on trials presented during states of low mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence did not differ from choice accuracy on yoked control trials, indicating that naturally occurring weak theta synchronization does not impair choice outcomes.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference between low coherence and yoked trials

claim: Relative to yoked control trials, trials initiated based on strong prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchrony were more likely to be correct compared to control trials on both working memory-dependent and -independent tasks.
source: Trials initiated based on strong prefrontal-hippocampal theta synchrony were more likely to be correct compared to control trials on both working memory-dependent and -independent tasks.
evidence: Stated as a result from the brain-machine interface experiment

claim: Prefrontal-thalamic neural interactions increased with prefrontal-hippocampal synchrony.
source: Prefrontal-thalamic neural interactions increased with prefrontal-hippocampal synchrony and optogenetic activation of the ventral midline thalamus primarily entrained prefrontal theta rhythms, but dynamically modulated synchrony.
evidence: Stated as a result from the experiments

claim: Relative to low coherence states, mPFC theta rhythms were stronger during high coherence states.
source: Relative to low coherence states, mPFC theta rhythms were stronger during high coherence states (Figure 3A and B; see Figure 2B for example LFP traces).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Hippocampal theta rhythms only exhibited a modest elevation in theta power relative to low coherence states.
source: Hippocampal theta rhythms only exhibited a modest elevation in theta power relative to low coherence states.
evidence: Stated as a result from offline data analysis

claim: mPFC theta rhythms were shifted toward higher frequencies during high coherence states (mean theta frequency = 5.8 Hz) relative to low coherence states (mean theta frequency = 5 Hz).
source: With respect to theta frequency, mPFC theta rhythms were shifted toward higher frequencies during high coherence states (mean theta frequency = 5.8 Hz) relative to low coherence states (mean theta frequency = 5 Hz) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: 6/8 rats showed higher theta frequency in the hippocampus during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states relative to low theta coherence states.
source: While there was no significant difference in hippocampal theta frequency, 6/8 rats showed higher theta frequency during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states (mean theta frequency during high coherence states = 7 Hz; mean theta frequency during low coherence states = 6.5 Hz).
evidence: Stated as a result from offline data analysis

claim: Relative to low coherence states, high coherence states were characterized by stronger hippocampal-to-mPFC theta directionality.
source: Relative to low coherence states, high coherence states were characterized by stronger hippocampal-to-mPFC theta directionality (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The high theta coherence states used to trigger spatial working memory trials were characterized by strong mPFC theta rhythms and hippocampal-to-mPFC theta directionality.
source: Thus, the high theta coherence states used to trigger spatial working memory trials were characterized by strong mPFC theta rhythms and hippocampal-to-mPFC theta directionality.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the offline data analysis

claim: Strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence during the delay was maintained throughout choice.
source: This latter result shows that strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence during the delay was maintained throughout choice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of theta coherence differences at pre-choice and post-choice entry

claim: Theta coherence values were predictive of future theta coherence values, but this effect slowly decayed over time.
source: While theta coherence values were predictive of future theta coherence values, this effect slowly decayed over time, indicating that despite some observations of periodicity, the fluctuations were largely non-periodical (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Despite some observations of periodicity, mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence fluctuations were largely non-periodical.
source: While theta coherence values were predictive of future theta coherence values, this effect slowly decayed over time, indicating that despite some observations of periodicity, the fluctuations were largely non-periodical (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: When the delay phase was fixed and predictable, strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events did not predict trial initiation.
source: However, when we examined the frequency of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events when the delay phase was fixed and predictable, strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events did not predict trial initiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events predict choice outcome, rather than trial onset.
source: When considered with the results above, mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events predict choice outcome, rather than trial onset.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that strong theta coherence events did not predict trial initiation in fixed delay conditions

claim: Initiation of trials during strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence enhanced choice accuracy on the conditional discrimination task.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that initiation of trials during strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence enhanced choice accuracy on the conditional discrimination task (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C

claim: mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence did not previously correlate with choice outcomes on the conditional discrimination task.
source: This finding was surprising given that mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence did not previously correlate with choice outcomes on the conditional discrimination task (Hallock et al., 2016), but consistent with increased mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence on a different cue-guided paradigm (Benchenane et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hallock et al., 2016

claim: Strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence is optimal for decision-making behavior regardless of whether working memory and mPFC/hippocampal function is necessary to perform a task.
source: Most importantly, these results show that strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence is optimal for decision-making behavior regardless of whether working memory and mPFC/hippocampal function is necessary to perform a task.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that strong theta coherence improved performance on both working memory-dependent and -independent tasks

claim: Past research showed that mPFC-hippocampal theta synchrony during choice was supported by the VMT.
source: Past research showed that mPFC-hippocampal theta synchrony during choice was supported by the VMT (Hallock et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hallock et al., 2016

claim: The VMT is anatomically connected with the mPFC and hippocampus.
source: The VMT is anatomically connected with the mPFC and hippocampus (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2002; McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Vertes et al., 2006; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Hoover and Vertes, 2012), providing a source of glutamatergic excitation to both structures (Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: The VMT provides a source of glutamatergic excitation to both the mPFC and hippocampus.
source: The VMT is anatomically connected with the mPFC and hippocampus (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2002; McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Vertes et al., 2006; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Hoover and Vertes, 2012), providing a source of glutamatergic excitation to both structures (Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019

claim: High theta coherence states were characterized by strong 6–9 Hz theta rhythms in the mPFC.
source: Corroborating the findings from our brain-machine interfacing experiment (Figures 2 and 3), high theta coherence states were characterized by strong 6–9 Hz theta rhythms in the mPFC (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: The magnitude change of theta power between high and low coherence states was strongest in the mPFC, followed by the VMT, then the hippocampus.
source: Intriguingly, the magnitude change of theta power between high and low coherence states was strongest in the mPFC, followed by the VMT, then the hippocampus (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Relative to low coherence epochs, the mPFC was differentially and simultaneously synchronized to the VMT and hippocampus during high coherence states.
source: Relative to low coherence epochs, the mPFC was differentially and simultaneously synchronized to the VMT and hippocampus during high coherence states (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: High coherence states were characterized by a stronger change in neural synchronization between the mPFC and VMT, relative to the VMT and hippocampus.
source: Moreover, high coherence states were characterized by a stronger change in neural synchronization between the mPFC and VMT, relative to the VMT and hippocampus (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claim: mPFC-VMT interactions may be particularly sensitive to mPFC-hippocampal synchronization.
source: This latter result suggested that mPFC-VMT interactions may be particularly sensitive to mPFC-hippocampal synchronization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mPFC-VMT synchronization changed more than VMT-hippocampal synchronization

claim: mPFC-VMT directionality was elevated during strong relative to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states.
source: In support of this conclusion, multivariate Granger prediction revealed that mPFC-VMT directionality was elevated during strong relative to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states (Figure 5G; middle panel).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: mPFC-hippocampal directionality was modulated by mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence magnitude.
source: mPFC-hippocampal directionality was also modulated by mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence magnitude.
evidence: Stated as a result from multivariate Granger prediction analysis

claim: Directionality between the VMT and hippocampus was minimally impacted by the magnitude of mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence.
source: However, directionality between the VMT and hippocampus was minimally impacted by the magnitude of mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: When comparing strong to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, there were no significant differences to theta phase entrainment of mPFC spikes to VMT and hippocampal theta.
source: When comparing strong to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, there were no significant differences to theta phase entrainment (Figure 5I) nor to spike-field coherence (Figure 5J) of mPFC spikes to VMT and hippocampal theta.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5I

claim: When comparing strong to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, there were no significant differences to spike-field coherence of mPFC spikes to VMT and hippocampal theta.
source: When comparing strong to weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, there were no significant differences to theta phase entrainment (Figure 5I) nor to spike-field coherence (Figure 5J) of mPFC spikes to VMT and hippocampal theta.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5J

claim: During strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, 8.9% and 7% of mPFC neurons were modulated by hippocampal theta and VMT theta, respectively.
source: During strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, 8.9% and 7% of mPFC neurons were modulated by hippocampal theta and VMT theta, respectively.
evidence: Stated as a result from spike-LFP analysis

claim: During weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, 4.4% and 2.3% of mPFC neurons were significantly modulated by hippocampal and VMT theta, respectively.
source: This contrasted with weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states, where 4.4% and 2.3% of mPFC neurons were significantly modulated by hippocampal and VMT theta, respectively (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5K

claim: The magnitude of mPFC-hippocampal theta synchronization was unrelated to global changes to mPFC spike entrainment to VMT and hippocampal theta rhythms.
source: These findings indicate that the magnitude of mPFC-hippocampal theta synchronization was unrelated to global changes to mPFC spike entrainment to VMT and hippocampal theta rhythms.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant differences in spike-phase entrainment and spike-field coherence

claim: Relative to low coherence states, states of high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence were associated with strong mPFC spike-phase locking to VMT and hippocampal theta rhythms in a small group of mPFC neurons.
source: Instead, relative to low coherence states, states of high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence were associated with strong mPFC spike-phase locking to VMT and hippocampal theta rhythms in a small group of mPFC neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that a small percentage of neurons showed significant modulation

claim: VMT theta rhythm stimulation increased the power of mPFC theta oscillations across all recording channels from a 64ch silicone probe targeting mPFC lamina.
source: VMT theta rhythm stimulation increased the power of mPFC theta oscillations across all recording channels from a 64ch silicone probe targeting mPFC lamina (Figure 6B and C; see Figure 6—figure supplement 2 as a companion figure to Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Stimulation of the VMT at 7, 15, or 30 Hz produced clear changes to the mPFC power spectrum.
source: Stimulation of the VMT at 7, 15, or 30 Hz produced clear changes to the mPFC power spectrum, while 4 Hz stimulation was more variable across shanks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H

claim: VMT stimulation at 4 Hz was more variable across shanks.
source: Stimulation of the VMT at 7, 15, or 30 Hz produced clear changes to the mPFC power spectrum, while 4 Hz stimulation was more variable across shanks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VMT at 7–8 Hz was largely disruptive to mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence.
source: Surprisingly, optogenetic activation of the VMT at 7–8 Hz was largely disruptive to mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–G), but was nonetheless capable of increasing mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence at unexpected frequencies (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–G

claim: VMT stimulation was capable of increasing mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence at unexpected frequencies.
source: Surprisingly, optogenetic activation of the VMT at 7–8 Hz was largely disruptive to mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–G), but was nonetheless capable of increasing mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence at unexpected frequencies (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E

claim: VMT stimulation was better capable of increasing mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence when timed with real-time monitoring of hippocampal oscillations and with sufficient activation.
source: Specifically, VMT stimulation was better capable of increasing mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence when timed with real-time monitoring of hippocampal oscillations and with sufficient activation.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the optogenetic experiments

claim: Square wave optogenetic stimulation of the VMT does not pose a viable approach to strengthen mPFC-hippocampal coherence without consideration of ongoing oscillatory dynamics.
source: While we expected VMT stimulation to strengthen mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence, these results indicate that square wave optogenetic stimulation of the VMT does not pose a viable approach to strengthen mPFC-hippocampal coherence without consideration of ongoing oscillatory dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VMT stimulation was largely disruptive to mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence

claim: VMT stimulation most effectively produces closely matched oscillations in the mPFC.
source: Instead, VMT stimulation most effectively produces closely matched oscillations in the mPFC, a finding with interesting implications for diseases characterized by a disrupted thalamic complex (Elvsåshagen et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the optogenetic experiments and supported by citation to Elvsåshagen et al., 2021

claim: Previous research showed that mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence was stronger when memory was used to guide choices.
source: Previous research showed that mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence was stronger when memory was used to guide choices (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Benchenane et al., 2010; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016), but this conclusion required correlating choice outcome with mPFC-hippocampal theta synchrony.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: The brain-machine interfacing experiments allowed implementation of various within-subject controls.
source: Our brain-machine interfacing experiments allowed us to implement various within-subject controls and we showed that trials initiated during states of strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence led to better task performance on two separate paradigms.
evidence: Stated as a description of the experimental approach

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the mPFC, VMT, or hippocampus did not impair conditional discrimination task performance in well-trained rats.
source: Likewise, past research showed that inactivation of the mPFC or the VMT did not disrupt conditional discrimination task performance in well-trained rats (Hallock et al., 2013b; Shaw et al., 2013), indicating that the mPFC-hippocampal network is not required for conditional discrimination task performance.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hallock et al., 2013b; Shaw et al., 2013

claim: The mPFC-hippocampal network is not required for conditional discrimination task performance.
source: Likewise, past research showed that inactivation of the mPFC or the VMT did not disrupt conditional discrimination task performance in well-trained rats (Hallock et al., 2013b; Shaw et al., 2013), indicating that the mPFC-hippocampal network is not required for conditional discrimination task performance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pharmacological inactivation did not impair task performance

claim: Pharmacological techniques, which work on the scale of minutes, may provide time for the brain to adapt to a disrupted mPFC-hippocampal network.
source: Given that the conditional discrimination task is dependent on the dorsal striatum, it is possible that pharmacological techniques, which work on the scale of minutes, provided time for the brain to adapt to a disrupted mPFC-hippocampal network.
evidence: Stated as a possible explanation for the discrepancy between pharmacological inactivation and brain-machine interfacing results

claim: Optogenetic suppression of the CA1 on a time scale similar to pharmacological agents did not impair the retrieval of a contextual fear memory.
source: In support of this view, Goshen et al., 2011, showed that optogenetic suppression of the CA1 on a time scale similar to pharmacological agents, like muscimol, did not impair the retrieval of a contextual fear memory.
evidence: Supported by citation to Goshen et al., 2011

claim: When optogenetic inactivation was temporally specific to the testing phase of the contextual fear memory paradigm, memory retrieval was disrupted.
source: However, when optogenetic inactivation was temporally specific to the testing phase of the contextual fear memory paradigm, memory retrieval was disrupted.
evidence: Stated as a result from Goshen et al., 2011

claim: The timescale of inactivation impacts the results and conclusions drawn from research.
source: These findings show that the timescale of inactivation impacts the results and conclusions drawn from research, raising the possibility that the mPFC-hippocampal network can indeed be beneficial to the performance of working memory-independent tasks.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of pharmacological and optogenetic inactivation results

claim: The mPFC-hippocampal network can be beneficial to the performance of working memory-independent tasks.
source: These findings show that the timescale of inactivation impacts the results and conclusions drawn from research, raising the possibility that the mPFC-hippocampal network can indeed be beneficial to the performance of working memory-independent tasks.
evidence: Stated as a possibility based on the experimental results

claim: The mPFC receives no direct projections from the dHPC.
source: Importantly, this latter assertion is supported by anatomy, as the mPFC receives no direct projections from the dHPC (Jay and Witter, 1991; Hoover and Vertes, 2007), but influences hippocampal neuronal activity via the thalamus (Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jay and Witter, 1991; Hoover and Vertes, 2007

claim: The mPFC influences hippocampal neuronal activity via the thalamus.
source: Importantly, this latter assertion is supported by anatomy, as the mPFC receives no direct projections from the dHPC (Jay and Witter, 1991; Hoover and Vertes, 2007), but influences hippocampal neuronal activity via the thalamus (Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 2015

claim: The VMT may coordinate mPFC-hippocampal neural interactions through cortico-thalamo-cortical looping mechanisms.
source: We suspect that the VMT may coordinate mPFC-hippocampal neural interactions through cortico-thalamo-cortical looping mechanisms, as the VMT projects directly to entorhinal cortex neurons that target the CA1 (Wouterlood, 1991) and modulates CA1 neurons with concurrent cortical activation (Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to Wouterlood, 1991 and Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2017

claim: The VMT projects directly to entorhinal cortex neurons that target the CA1.
source: We suspect that the VMT may coordinate mPFC-hippocampal neural interactions through cortico-thalamo-cortical looping mechanisms, as the VMT projects directly to entorhinal cortex neurons that target the CA1 (Wouterlood, 1991) and modulates CA1 neurons with concurrent cortical activation (Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wouterlood, 1991

claim: The VMT modulates CA1 neurons with concurrent cortical activation.
source: We suspect that the VMT may coordinate mPFC-hippocampal neural interactions through cortico-thalamo-cortical looping mechanisms, as the VMT projects directly to entorhinal cortex neurons that target the CA1 (Wouterlood, 1991) and modulates CA1 neurons with concurrent cortical activation (Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2017

claim: Mediodorsal thalamus is known to sustain mPFC neuronal activity.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, mediodorsal thalamus is known to sustain mPFC neuronal activity (Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017), and the VMT supports mPFC firing and mPFC-hippocampal synchronization (Hallock et al., 2016; Jayachandran et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017

claim: The VMT supports mPFC firing and mPFC-hippocampal synchronization.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, mediodorsal thalamus is known to sustain mPFC neuronal activity (Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017), and the VMT supports mPFC firing and mPFC-hippocampal synchronization (Hallock et al., 2016; Jayachandran et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hallock et al., 2016; Jayachandran et al., 2023

claim: When examining all mPFC neurons, there were no differences to spike-LFP synchronization between strong and weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events.
source: When examining all mPFC neurons, we found no differences to spike-LFP synchronization between strong and weak mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events.
evidence: Stated as a result from spike-LFP analysis

claim: There was a rather small increase to the percentage of theta modulated units in the mPFC during strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states.
source: Instead, we found a rather small increase to the percentage of theta modulated units in the mPFC.
evidence: Stated as a result from spike-LFP analysis

claim: LFP signal coherence between a sending and receiving structure can be explained by a sending structures signal power and strength of projectors and can emerge without changes to spike entrainment in the receiving structure.
source: For example, Schneider et al., 2021, showed that LFP signal coherence between a sending and receiving structure can be explained by a sending structures signal power and strength of projectors and can emerge without changes to spike entrainment in the receiving structure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2021

claim: The ventral hippocampus and VMT are necessary for mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence.
source: Given that the ventral hippocampus and VMT are necessary for mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016), we suspect that afferents from these structures contribute significantly to mPFC-hippocampal oscillatory synchronization.
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016

claim: Afferents from the ventral hippocampus and VMT contribute significantly to mPFC-hippocampal oscillatory synchronization.
source: Given that the ventral hippocampus and VMT are necessary for mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (O'Neill et al., 2013; Hallock et al., 2016), we suspect that afferents from these structures contribute significantly to mPFC-hippocampal oscillatory synchronization.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on the necessity of ventral hippocampus and VMT for mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence

claim: mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events may represent short temporal periods of neural communication, rather than scaffolding communication.
source: When taken together, mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence events may represent short temporal periods of neural communication, rather than scaffolding communication.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that coherence can emerge without changes to spike entrainment

claim: A recent study found that inducing states of theta synchrony between frontal and temporal regions via transcranial alternating-current stimulation rescued age-related memory impairments in human participants.
source: Consistent with our work, a recent study found that inducing states of theta synchrony between frontal and temporal regions via transcranial alternating-current stimulation rescued age-related memory impairments in human participants (Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019

claim: Tapping into pre-existing neural dynamics holds significant promise for improving memory.
source: Our findings suggest that tapping into pre-existing neural dynamics holds significant promise for improving memory.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experimental results

claim: Non-invasive stimulation techniques prior to therapy, paired with synchrony-dependent attention or working memory practice via brain-machine interfacing, could pose a viable intervention to improve cognitive deficits.
source: We hypothesize that non-invasive stimulation techniques prior to therapy, paired with synchrony-dependent attention or working memory practice via brain-machine interfacing, could pose a viable intervention to improve cognitive deficits.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental results

claim: The use of brain-machine interfacing holds significant promise for clinical and neuroscientific advance.
source: In closing, the use of brain-machine interfacing holds significant promise for clinical and neuroscientific advance.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the research

claim: Prefrontal theta power (6–9 Hz) was significantly greater during high coherence epochs relative to low coherence epochs.
source: Prefrontal theta power (6–9 Hz) was significantly greater during high coherence epochs relative to low coherence epochs (t(7) = 5.3, ci = 0.14–0.37, padj(x2)=0.002).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Hippocampal theta power was stronger on high coherence compared to low coherence trials.
source: Hippocampal theta power was stronger on high coherence compared to low coherence trials (t(7) = 2.47, ci = 0.006–0.28, padj(x2)=0.08, pnot-adj=0.0427).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The frequency of prefrontal theta oscillations was significantly higher during high coherence states relative to low coherence states.
source: The frequency of prefrontal theta oscillations was significantly higher during high coherence states relative to low coherence states (PFC: t(7) = 3.08, padj(x2)=0.036, ci = 0.16–1.3; hippocampus: t(7) = 1.8, ci = –0.17 to 1.3, p=0.11).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Hippocampal-to-prefrontal theta directionality was significantly stronger during high theta coherence states relative to low theta coherence states.
source: Hippocampal-to-prefrontal theta directionality was significantly stronger during high theta coherence states relative to low theta coherence states (t(7) = 3.53, ci = [0.12–0.64], padj(x3)=0.029) and was significantly stronger than Granger prediction in the prefrontal-to-hippocampal direction (t(7) = 3.33, ci = 0.097–0.57, padj(x3)=0.038).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Hippocampal-to-prefrontal theta directionality was significantly stronger than Granger prediction in the prefrontal-to-hippocampal direction during high theta coherence states.
source: Hippocampal-to-prefrontal theta directionality was significantly stronger during high theta coherence states relative to low theta coherence states (t(7) = 3.53, ci = [0.12–0.64], padj(x3)=0.029) and was significantly stronger than Granger prediction in the prefrontal-to-hippocampal direction (t(7) = 3.33, ci = 0.097–0.57, padj(x3)=0.038).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Theta coherence at choice entry was significantly stronger on trials triggered by high coherence relative to trials triggered during low coherence.
source: Theta coherence at choice entry was significantly stronger on trials triggered by high coherence relative to trials triggered during low coherence (see Supplementary file 1b for raw and corrected p-values).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3H

claim: There was a main effect of brain region on the coherence difference score between high and low coherence epochs.
source: There was a main effect of brain region on the coherence difference score (F(2,65) = 20.8; p<0.001; one-way ANOVA) with each brain area showing higher theta power during high coherence states relative to low coherence states (PFC: p<0.001; VMT; p<0.001; HPC: p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Each brain area (PFC, VMT, HPC) showed higher theta power during high coherence states relative to low coherence states.
source: There was a main effect of brain region on the coherence difference score (F(2,65) = 20.8; p<0.001; one-way ANOVA) with each brain area showing higher theta power during high coherence states relative to low coherence states (PFC: p<0.001; VMT; p<0.001; HPC: p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: mPFC-VMT theta coherence changed more drastically with mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence magnitude compared to VMT-HPC theta coherence.
source: mPFC-VMT theta coherence changed more drastically with mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence magnitude (mPFC-VMT: p<0.001; VMT-HPC: p<0.001; mPFC-VMT vs VMT-HPC: p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: Delay duration on brain-machine interfacing trials was significantly shorter when compared to the delay duration on random delay trials with coincident strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence.
source: Delay duration on brain-machine interfacing trials was significantly shorter when compared to the delay duration on random delay trials with coincident strong mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence (t(7) = –3.8, ci = –6.4 to –1.6, p=0.006; paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Low coherence trials showed significantly lower IdPhi (behavioral complexity) relative to yoked trials.
source: Low coherence trials showed significantly lower IdPhi relative to yoked trials (t(7) = –2.5, ci = [–68.36, –1.9]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Trials initiated during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states led to better task performance when compared to yoked control trials on the conditional discrimination task.
source: Trials initiated during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states led to better task performance when compared to yoked control trials (t(15) = 2.23, ci = 0.29–12.87, p(p.c.)=0.04) or when compared to trials triggered following a random delay (t(15) = 3.8, ci = 4.7–16.6, p(x2)=0.002).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Trials initiated during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states led to better task performance when compared to trials triggered following a random delay on the conditional discrimination task.
source: Trials initiated during high mPFC-hippocampal theta coherence states led to better task performance when compared to yoked control trials (t(15) = 2.23, ci = 0.29–12.87, p(p.c.)=0.04) or when compared to trials triggered following a random delay (t(15) = 3.8, ci = 4.7–16.6, p(x2)=0.002).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VMT produced a large negative deflection in the mPFC voltage.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of the VMT produced a large negative deflection in the mPFC voltage (Figure 6D), but reliably increased mPFC oscillation power that closely matched the VMT stimulation frequency across all animals and sessions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VMT reliably increased mPFC oscillation power that closely matched the VMT stimulation frequency across all animals and sessions.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of the VMT produced a large negative deflection in the mPFC voltage (Figure 6D), but reliably increased mPFC oscillation power that closely matched the VMT stimulation frequency across all animals and sessions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1
